newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian bond mood grim as support gives in.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian bond mood grim as support gives in.

text.p: *Australian bond yields spiked to their highest level this year as key support on futures caved in, and as the market became highly nervous over this week's data and events offshore.
*January retail trade, building approvals due Tuesday.
Australian bond yields spiked to their highest level this year as key support on futures caved in, and as the market became extremely nervous over this week's data and events offshore.

Traders said that offshore selling at the short end spilled over to long-dated stocks and the move snowballed from there, with March 10-year bond futures breaking through last week's after hours low of 92.205.
And with any hope of an easing in policy now ditched, the three-year benchmark bond, the April 2000 stock, sprung through 7.0 percent for the first time since September 1996.

Today's data saw the January balance of goods and services, which replaced the monthly current account report, and showed a A$63 million deficit compared with a A$235 million surplus in December. Also released was the fourth quarter stocks report, which rose 1.2 percent.

"Today's data add to the impression from other recent releases that the pace of activity in late 1996-early 1997 was not as subdued as originally perceived," said Michael Blythe, senior economist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia.
While attention will be on Wednesday's GDP for confirmation of this, Tuesday's data will give a more up to date picture.

"Tuesday's household spending data is probably more important in a forward looking sense. We expect a rise in building approvals to confirm that the housing leg of the recovery is intact, and sharp rebound in retail trade," Blythe's CBA added.
Median forecasts for January retail trade centre on a 1.5 percent rise, while building approvals are seen up 2.0 percent, with both having dropped 1.0 percent in December.
Adding to the local market's bleak tone are concerns over this week's key events in the U.S., which kick off today with the February National Association Purchasing Management index.

Yield spreads blew out sharply as the local market also factored in further weakness in U.S. Treasuries this week with Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan due to give the second leg of his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on Wednesday. Friday also sees the key non-farm payrolls report for February.
